Abstract The accurate diﬀerentiation of pulmonary lesions (nodule/mass) is crucial for selecting appropri-
ate treatment strategies, particularly for distinguishing benign lesions such as hamartoma and tuberculoma
from malignancies like non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study investigates the use of machine
learning (ML) models, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), and CatBoost (CB), to iden-
tify key predictors of nodules type based on computed tomography (CT) imaging features. We analyzed
CT data from 363 patients with conﬁrmed diagnoses of hamartoma, tuberculoma, or NSCLC to evalu-
ate the models’ predictive performance and identify the most signiﬁcant diagnostic features. The models
demonstrated high accuracy, sensitivity, and speciﬁcity, with DT and CB models highlighting changes
in surrounding tissue as primary indicators, whereas RF integrated additional predictors, providing a
nuanced classiﬁcation framework. These ﬁndings suggest that ML models can enhance diagnostic accuracy
for lung lesions and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures, although further validation in larger cohorts
is recommended.
1 Introduction
Incidentally discovered pulmonary lesions (“nodules”<30 mm and “mass” >30 mm) on computed tomography
(CT) present a signiﬁcant medical challenge, as they require further investigation to determine their nature [1–3].
Non-invasive diagnosis of solitary pulmonary nodules with accuracy comparable to or close to that of a biopsy
remains a key issue in thoracic radiology. The management strategy for patients with a solitary pulmonary nodules
(and mass) primarily depends on the presumptive diagnosis, where diﬀerential diagnosis concerning the malignancy
level of the identiﬁed nodule/mass is almost always required.
Currently, numerous protocols have been proposed to classify such lesions as malignant or benign [1–3]. Despite
their widespread use, these protocols exhibit several limitations, one of which is the over-diagnosis of lung cancer.
In a study [4] published by the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) research group in the United States,
between August 2002 and April 2004, 53,454 high-risk individuals for lung cancer were enrolled across 33 medical
centers. Participants were randomly assigned to undergo three annual screenings using either low-dose CT (26,722
participants) or single-view chest radiography (26,732). CT results led to a total of 673 “signiﬁcant” diagnostic
interventions, which ruled out lung cancer in 164 cases (24.4%). In addition to being costly, these so-called excessive
invasive procedures led to at least one complication in 26 cases (15.9%), and two cases (1.2%) resulted in death
within 60 days of the invasive procedure [4].
In the past decade, numerous machine learning models have been developed for the detection of pulmonary
lesions. A recent comprehensive review [5] discusses the primary applications of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) in
diagnosing pulmonary nodules and lung cancer using computed tomography (CT) and chest radiography. It has
been demonstrated that deep learning (DL) networks, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNN), can

achieve performance comparable to that of radiologists, and in some cases, even surpass them in terms of detection
speed and accuracy. Algorithms capable of predicting nodule malignancy have also been explored, potentially
reducing the number of unnecessary follow-up studies. In lung cancer diagnostics, AI is further applied to non-
invasive assessment of tumor histological subtypes, mutation prediction, and outcome prognostication, which is
especially valuable for treatment planning. Another review [6] primarily examines algorithms that utilize feature-
based methods, such as support vector machines (SVM), which demonstrate high accuracy. However, deep learning
oﬀers the advantage of bypassing the manual feature selection stage and progressively improves accuracy as training
data increases. Despite the abundance of developed models and their eﬀective use in certain local hospitals,
the systematic implementation of machine learning (ML) algorithms in clinical practice currently faces several
challenges. These include algorithmic complexity, their opaque ”black box” nature, and limited data on their
impact on healthcare quality. Additionally, the lack of a standardized approach to evaluating algorithm eﬃcacy
hinders the development of a uniﬁed diagnostic protocol for clinicians [5, 6].
Models have also been developed to assist general practitioners in assessing individual lung cancer risk, using
approaches such as multivariable logistic regression-most notably the Mayo Clinic model [7]-and Bayesian analy-
sis, with the SPN model [8] being the most recognized. In addition to radiological characteristics, these models
incorporated factors such as smoking status, age, presence of hemoptysis, and any history of malignancies prior to
examination [7, 8]. However, these models have not seen widespread adoption in clinical practice.
It is worth noting that the developed models do not diﬀerentiate between benign processes, which sometimes
require close monitoring and distinct treatment approaches. For example, a pulmonary hamartoma does not require
surgical intervention, in contrast to a malignant lesions [7]. Meanwhile, a tuberculoma requires microbiological
or morphological conﬁrmation, followed by monitoring and a course of anti-tuberculosis therapy. A pulmonary
hamartoma is one of the most common true benign pulmonary lesions, typically exhibiting distinct pathological
features on chest computed tomography (CT) [8]. These features often include a combination of calciﬁcations and
fat within the hamartoma structure. However, this combination is observed in approximately 21% of cases, while
isolated calciﬁcations are seen in around 25% and fat alone in 30–60% of cases [9, 10]. This variability necessitates
that radiologists carefully assess additional CT features and consider their prevalence in other types of pulmonary
lesions. For example, calciﬁcation within the context of a solitary pulmonary nodule are also found in tuberculomas-
infectious granulomas caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis [11]. Tuberculomas are the leading benign process
among solitary pulmonary nodules [12]. However, in cases of delayed detection, there is a risk of reactivation of
the inﬂammatory process, potentially progressing to active pulmonary tuberculosis [13]. In some cases, pulmonary
hamartomas exhibit CT characteristics similar to malignant lesions, leading to unnecessary invasive procedures,
including lung resection. Malignancies are conﬁrmed postoperatively in only 15% of such cases following these
surgical interventions [14].
In this study, we analyzed data from patients with benign (hamartoma, tuberculoma) and malignant (non-
small cell lung cancer) lung lesions to identify key CT characteristics that facilitate diﬀerentiation between these
diagnoses. Machine learning models based on decision tree approaches were employed to determine which features
(both CT and general clinical characteristics) are most signiﬁcantly associated with malignancy. These ﬁndings
are aimed at enhancing diagnostic accuracy and, with further reﬁnement of such models, potentially reducing the
number of unnecessary invasive procedures.
2 Materials and methods
The study has been conducted at the Saint-Petersburg State Research Institute of Phthisiopulmonology. All
patients had signed a written consent for storage of anonymized processed clinical material. This material’s usage
for the study has been approved by the Independent Ethics Committee (reference number 2024№126.3, data
25.01.2024) at the Saint-Petersburg State Research Institute of Phthisiopulmonology.
2.1 Patient selection
We analyzed 363 computed tomography scans (CT), including data from 142 patients with conﬁrmed pulmonary
hamartomas (PH) from 2013 to 2023, 128 patients with conﬁrmed tuberculomas (TB) from 2013 to 2023, and 93
patients who underwent surgery for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) from 2018 to 2022.
The inclusion criteria for patients with the listed pathologies were as follows: (1) nodule veriﬁcation: for pul-
monary hamartomas, histological conﬁrmation or a monitoring period of more than 600 days in patients with
typical pulmonary hamartomas (with fat present in the structure) [11]; for tuberculomas, etiological veriﬁcation;
and for malignant nodules, histological conﬁrmation; (2) availability of native CT scans, including preoperative
scans in cases of surgical intervention. Exclusion criteria included: (1) inadequate image quality (motion artifacts
or high radiation hardness artifacts); (2) central or endobronchial nodule location. Additionally, in the pulmonary

hamartoma cohort, CT scans showing multiple nodules or other pulmonary lesions were excluded. Nodules with
destructive structural changes were excluded from the TB and NSCLC cohorts.
2.2 CT and clinical characteristics
Clinical data included patient characteristics such as sex, age, pathology type (LM), and lesion location within the
lung (Lung) and its segment (LS). CT features included nodule size (Size) and nodule type (TN). All nodules were
classiﬁed into three types: solid lung nodule, part-solid lung nodule, and ground-glass nodule. Additional features
assessed included fat content (fat), calciﬁcation presence (calciﬁcation), nodule margin clarity and smoothness
(CC, CF), and changes in the surrounding lung tissue (changeST).
We also incorporated nodule positioning relative to the bronchus according to the Tsuboi classiﬁcation (tsuboi)
[15, 16] and evaluation of the bronchus triangle sign (bronchus) [17] as an indirect indicator of wall changes in the
bronchus adjacent to the nodule. CT features were retrospectively analyzed by two radiologists. The density range
for fat inclusions within the nodules was standardized between –120 and –40 HU [12]. Final decisions regarding
Tsuboi classiﬁcation and bronchus triangle sign assignments were reached by consensus. Due to the retrospective
nature of the data, we were unable to analyze factors such as smoking status or history of malignancy.
2.3 Model development
To build models using the Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and CatBoost (CB) methods, we employed
the PyCharm (Python version 3.8) development environment along with the Pandas and Sklearn libraries. The
modules RandomForestClassiﬁer [18], DecisionTreeClassiﬁer [18], and CatBoostClassiﬁer [19] were imported for
each respective model.
The following parameters were applied to the Random Forest and Decision Tree methods: (i) The criterion for
split quality assessment was set to Gini; (ii) The maximum tree depth was set to 3; (iii) For the Random Forest
model, the number of trees in the forest was speciﬁed as 25, identiﬁed as optimal for eﬀective modeling; (iv) for
Decision tree model we used parameter splitter: the strategy for splitting nodes. It can be ”best” for selecting
the best split or ”random” for random selection. The default is ”best.” To build the model using the CatBoost
approach, we applied the following parameters: (i) iterations: the number of trees constructed, set to an optimal
value of 10 in our case; (ii) learning_rate: the model’s learning rate; (iii) tree depth, which was set to 4.
For the RF and DT models, an optimal split of 40% for the test set and 60% for model training was selected,
as this ratio ensured more eﬃcient model performance. For the CB model, however, the most eﬀective split was
found to be 30% for testing and 70% for training. Also it should be noted, that all clinical characteristics beside
age and size of nodule are categorical. Since the simulation required accounting for all factors speciﬁed by the
clinical inclusion criteria, a preliminary connectivity analysis (using the FAMD method) was not performed.
3 Results
We developed three binomial models using each of the three approaches (RF, DT and CB) to diﬀerentiate between
oncology (NSCLC)-hamartoma, oncology (NSCLC)-tuberculoma, and hamartoma-tuberculoma cases.
3.1 Tuberculoma + NSCLC
The decision tree model results are presented in Table 1 (second column) and Fig. 1. As shown in the table, patient
age is one of the primary predictors. When the patient’s age is ≦49.5, there is a 92% probability that the patient
may be diagnosed with tuberculoma (TB), as shown in left branch in Fig. 1. The second-level predictors for this
model are contour clarity (CC) and the Tsuboi index. If CC = 0 (indicating clear contours), there is a ≈97%
probability that the patient will present with TB. When the Tsuboi index is < 2, the NSCLC class is predominant.
Otherwise, the TB class prevails.
In the random forest (RF) model, as in the previous model, patient age is the primary predictor (see Table 2
and Fig. 2). If age ≦52.5, there is tuberculoma can be predicted with an accuracy of nearly 90%. The second-
and the third-level predictors are lung tsuboi. The second-level predictors are Size and Lung. When Lung = 0,
meaning the lesion is observed in the right lung (1 indicates the left lung), there is an 83% probability that the
patient has cancer. For patients aged ≦52.5 with a higher likelihood of TB and a nodule/mass size ≦40 mm,
there is an 84% probability that the patient has TB. It is worth noting that, compared to the decision tree (DT)
model, a greater number of clinical factors contribute to distinguishing cancer from tuberculoma in this model,
with the relative importance of each factor balanced proportionally (see Table 2, Column 2).

In the CatBoost model, age remains one of the most important factors (see Table 3). However, calciﬁcation
(CL), accounting for 11%, emerges as a second-level predictor, which is generally characteristic of tuberculoma.
The signiﬁcance of changes in surrounding lesion tissue (CSLT) is elevated compared to the RF model, contributing
approximately 10%.
3.2 Hamartoma + NSCLC
In the decision tree model for diﬀerentiating hamartoma from cancer, changes in surrounding lesion tissue (CSLT)
are the top predictor (see Table 1). If CSLT = 0 (indicating no surrounding tissue changes), there is a 62%
probability that the detected nodule/mass can be classiﬁed as hamartoma. Second-level predictors include contour
clarity (CC) and contour ﬂatness (CF). When CC = 0 (indicating well-deﬁned nodule boundaries), the lesion can
be attributed to hamartomas (PH) with an 86% probability. If CF = 1, indicating a nodular surface, there is an
89% probability of diagnosing cancer. Age, lung segment (LS), and size are also signiﬁcant factors. For example,
regardless of nodule size, if CC = 0, there is almost a 90% probability of classifying the lesion as hamartoma.
In both the RF and CatBoost (CB) models, changes in surrounding tissue remain the primary predictor. However,
in the random forest model (Table 2, Column 3), the second-level predictors are calciﬁcation and contour ﬂatness
(CF). The absence of calciﬁcation indicates an 81% probability of a cancer diagnosis, while CF = 0 classiﬁes the
lesion as hamartoma with an 88% probability, which aligns with the decision tree model. In the CatBoost model,
the second-level predictors are lesion size and the presence of fat deposits (see Table 3, Column 3).
3.3 Hamartoma + tuberculoma
The comparison of data for hamartoma and tuberculoma was of particular interest, as both of these benign lesions
are challenging to identify, especially at early stages.
In the decision tree (DT) model (Fig. 3, Table 1), as well as in the CatBoost (CB) model (Table 3), changes in
surrounding lesion tissue (CSLT) serve as the primary predictor, consistent with previous models. If CSLT = 0
(indicating no changes), there is a 57% probability that the nodule can be classiﬁed as hamartoma. Second-level
predictors are age and fat presence. If fat = 0 (indicating absence), there is a 89% probability that the nodule
can be classiﬁed as tuberculoma, as the presence of fat is a key medical characteristic for hamartoma. If there are
no surrounding tissue changes and age ≦38.5, there is a 92% probability that the nodule can be diagnosed as
hamartoma.
In the context of the random forest model, the situation diﬀers somewhat from the aforementioned models. The
ﬁrst-level predictor is age. If age ≦43.5 years, the node can be classiﬁed as a hamartoma with a probability of
51%. The second-level predictors are fat and size. If the patient’s age ≦43.5 years and the fat value = 0 (absent),
the node can be classiﬁed as a tuberculoma with a probability of 85%. Conversely, if the patient’s age > 43.5 years
and the size of the nodule ≦10.5 mm, the node can be classiﬁed as a hamartoma with a probability of 78%. It
should be noted that in the CatBoost model, the third-level predictors are size and the segment of the lung where
the nodule is detected.

were conducted, providing a comprehensive understanding of their performance. The analysis results indicated

Accuracy, representing the proportion of correct predictions among all classiﬁcations, exceeded 80% for each
model. Sensitivity, which indicates the model’s ability to correctly identify positive cases, also showed comparable
results, reaching values above 70%. This suggests that all models are signiﬁcantly capable of detecting nodules
that require attention and further clinical investigation.
Speciﬁcity, which demonstrates the model’s ability to accurately identify negative cases, was similarly high,
indicating a minimal number of false-positive results. Importantly, the diﬀerences in metrics between the models
were found to be insigniﬁcant, allowing us to conclude that all models exhibit comparable eﬀectiveness in the
context of our study.
4 Discussion
Thus, in the considered models of TB/NSCLC diﬀerentiation, patient age was identiﬁed as an important predictor
in the diﬀerential diagnosis between an oncological lesion and a tuberculoma. Although both cancer and tubercu-
losis can occur across all age groups, cancer is more frequently detected in older patients. The ﬁrst-level predictor
(age less than 49.5 years) indicates a need to consider tuberculoma as a potential diagnosis for the lesion, aligning
with the recommended age threshold for lung cancer screening [20]. The signiﬁcance of age is further supported

guidelines [3].
For patients under 49.5 years, the most signiﬁcant features indicating tuberculosis as the lesion etiology included
a lesion size of less than 41.5 mm and well-deﬁned margins. For patients over 49.5 years, key criteria suggesting an
oncological nature of the nodule/mass were a Type 1 or 2 bronchial involvement according to Tsuboi’s classiﬁcation-
indicating a connection between the lesion and the bronchus-and the absence of calciﬁcation within the lesion.
The identiﬁcation of the right lung as a third-level predictor for classifying a lesion as tuberculoma is unclear and
warrants further investigation with larger samples.
When comparing the DT, RF, and CB models, age remains the most critical predictor, reducing the likelihood of
lung cancer in patients under 52.5 years, consistent with the DT model and modern lung cancer screening criteria.
Predictors that increased the likelihood of tuberculosis included a lesion size of less than 40 mm and well-deﬁned
margins. Unlike the DT model, additional predictors emerged in this analysis, including contour irregularity, while
bronchial involvement and calciﬁcation were not listed. The criterion of lesion location in either lung remains
uncertain, as previous literature has not established a link between lung side and detected pathology (cancer,
tuberculosis).
In the diﬀerential diagnosis between hamartoma and lung cancer within the context of the models discussed, the
ﬁrst-level predictor is the presence of changes in the surrounding tissue. This ﬁnding aligns with the diﬀerential
diagnosis between hamartoma and tuberculoma, as it reﬂects the diﬀerent growth patterns of these lesions. Invasion
in lung cancer often results in alterations in surrounding tissues, whereas hamartomas generally do not cause such
changes.
Second-level predictors include the clarity of lesion margins and the presence or absence of contour irregularities.
According to the literature, these characteristics diﬀer in prevalence between the two conditions under consider-
ation. Third-level predictors include lesion size, patient age, and location in the upper lung lobes. The model
establishes a clear diagnostic sequence: a lesion in unaﬀected surrounding tissue, with a smooth contour, is highly
likely to be a hamartoma, whereas the presence of irregular margins prompts age as the next diagnostic consider-
ation. Literature suggests that the median age of aﬀected patients diﬀers between these diseases, and the model
identiﬁes the age at which this predictor is most signiﬁcant. Conversely, a rounded lesion in altered surrounding
tissue, located in the upper lung regions with an unclear margin, is more likely to be cancer than a hamartoma,
consistent with established diagnostic approaches. Analysis of the RF model indicated that the left or right lung
in which the lesion is located emerged as a signiﬁcant feature; however, this ﬁnding currently lacks explanation
and corroboration from other statistical data.
Of particular interest are the models distinguishing hamartoma from tuberculoma, where in both the DT and
CB models, changes in the surrounding tissue serve as the primary predictor. This is entirely reasonable, as the
growth pattern of hamartoma typically does not aﬀect surrounding tissue unless there is a concurrent pathology,
such as an inﬂammatory process. Tuberculosis, as an infectious disease, often involves changes beyond the primary
lesion. One of the most critical second-level predictors is the presence of fat-density inclusions, which, according
to the literature, are speciﬁc to hamartomas and are not expected in tuberculomas. The selection of additional
predictors is somewhat challenging to interpret from a medical perspective and may be inﬂuenced by a small subset
of patients who did not meet the primary criteria.
In examining the RF model, important predictors include age-speciﬁcally, 38.5–43.5 years for hamartoma, which
aligns with statistics indicating a peak incidence of hamartomas around age 40, while tuberculosis peaks in younger
patients. Higher-level predictors also include the presence of fat inclusions and lesion size. Changes in surrounding
tissue appear twice as third-level predictors. Thus, all models rely on the same key parameters, underscoring the
importance of these two features (changes in surrounding tissue and fat inclusions). However, the CB and RF
models identify fewer predictors that are less readily explained from a medical standpoint.
In summary, an analysis of all models suggests that for the diﬀerential diagnosis of lung lesions and masses,
especially in distinguishing between tuberculoma and cancer, factors such as patient age, lesion size, and margin
deﬁnition should be considered. As for the dependence of diﬀerentiation between pathologies on factors such as
the lung segment or the speciﬁc lung in which the lesion is detected, this requires a larger sample size and more
detailed analysis.

5 Conclusion
We have constructed and tested machine learning (ML) models for the diﬀerential diagnosis of lung nodules, specif-
ically for distinguishing between benign (hamartoma, tuberculoma) and malignant (non-small cell lung cancer)
nodules. By utilizing models based on Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), and CatBoost (CB) methods,
we identiﬁed key predictors such as patient age, lesion size, contour clarity, and the presence of fat inclusions that
can signiﬁcantly improve diagnostic accuracy.
Patient age emerged as one of the most signiﬁcant predictors, particularly in distinguishing tuberculoma from
lung cancer, where younger patients more frequently exhibit benign lesions. In the DT and CB models, changes in
the surrounding tissue were identiﬁed as primary indicators of a benign nature, whereas the RF model integrated
additional predictors, providing a more reﬁned classiﬁcation. All three models demonstrated high levels of accuracy,
sensitivity, and speciﬁcity, conﬁrming their eﬀectiveness in identifying the nature of lung lesions.
Thus, integrating ML algorithms into clinical practice may substantially improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce
the number of unnecessary invasive procedures. It should be noted that in the future, when considering a mul-
timodal model that accounts for three diseases simultaneously, a more detailed investigation of the relationships
between both continuous and categorical factors should be conducted. Such an analysis, particularly with the
inclusion of new data, would simplify complex datasets, uncover hidden patterns, and lay the groundwork for a
more thorough and targeted analysis. It allows also to validate mentioned above ﬁndings and enhance the reliability
and clinical applicability of the proposed models.

Abstract: The accurate diﬀerentiation of pulmonary lesions (nodule/mass) is crucial for selecting appropri- ate treatment strategies, particularly for distinguishing benign lesions such as hamartoma and tuberculoma from malignancies like non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) models, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), and CatBoost (CB), to iden- tify key predictors of nodules type based on computed tomography (CT) imaging features. We analyzed CT data from 363 patients with conﬁrmed diagnoses of hamartoma, tuberculoma, or NSCLC to evalu- ate the models’ predictive performance and identify the most signiﬁcant diagnostic features. The models demonstrated high accuracy, sensitivity, and speciﬁcity, with DT and CB models highlighting changes in surrounding tissue as primary indicators, whereas RF integrated additional predictors, providing a nuanced classiﬁcation framework. These ﬁndings suggest that ML models can enhance diagnostic accuracy for lung lesions and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures, although further validation in larger cohorts is recommended.
